title: Six students wait a year to ask
hookLine: six seekers arrive at a sage's door with their questions ready, and he tells them to wait a year
carry: tapas, brahmacharya and faith, then the question

cards: You've finally got a meeting with the expert. You walk in with your list of questions, and before you can open your mouth, they say: come back in a year.
The Prashna Upanishad opens with six serious people who come to a great teacher, wood for his fire in their hands, and that is roughly what he tells them. Prashna means question.
The whole Upanishad is built from the questions they ask. But first, they have to wait.

teach.b: Tradition places the Prashna in the Atharva Veda. It names its six students one by one: Sukesha Bharadvaja. Satyakama Shaibya.
Gargya Sauryayani. Kausalya Ashvalayana. Bhargava of Vidarbha.

And Kabandhi Katyayana. They were devoted to Brahman, the text says, grounded in it, seeking the highest. And they came to the sage Pippalada, fuel for his fire in hand, sure he could tell them everything.
Pippalada says: stay one more year, with tapas, with brahmacharya, and with shraddha. Discipline, a disciplined life of study, and faith. Then ask whatever you like.

teach.h: IF WE KNOW, WE'LL TELL YOU.
teach.b: And then the line that makes this teacher worth listening to: if we know, we'll tell you all of it. If we know. A great sage, six eager students, and he doesn't promise answers.
This is the heart of a relationship Hindus still keep: guru and shishya, teacher and student. The student arrives with fuel in hand, offering to tend the teacher's fire.
The teacher asks for readiness before the deepest teaching. It lives on wherever Hindus learn from a guru: Vedanta, Sanskrit, classical music, dance. Think about what the year does.
A question asked the day it occurs to you is often a reflex.
A question carried through a year of practice has had time to become real. Some answer themselves. The ones still standing are worth a teacher's time.
So when a teacher says not yet, it may not be a door closing. It may be the year Pippalada asked for. In the coming days, each student asks one question.

how: In traditional Hindu learning, a student lives with or near the teacher and studies for long periods before being taught the deepest texts; some Vedanta teachers today still ask students to study and practice before taking up the Upanishads.

games.q: you ask the teacher at your temple's Gita class a big question on your first night. he smiles: come every week for a year, then ask me anything. what's he doing?
o: gatekeeping; a real teacher answers right away.
what Pippalada did: a year of discipline, study and faith first, so the question is ready.
checking whether you can pay for private lessons.
games.why: Pippalada asked six seekers for one more year of tapas, brahmacharya and shraddha, then promised: if we know, we'll tell you all. that's the guru-shishya way.

practice: Let the body settle, and when the urge comes to move, check something or get on with the day, notice it and stay: that's a small tapas. One breath, then the next.
If a question rises, let it stand at the door, fuel in hand, until later.

wordCard.voice: Six students. The seekers of the Prashna Upanishad, told by the sage Pippalada to live a year in discipline and faith before asking, and promised only: if we know, we'll tell you.

orig.note: Sanskrit praśna, question: the Prashna Upanishad is built from six students' six questions.

carryVoice: Take this with you: tapas, brahmacharya and faith, then the question. Tomorrow, the year is up, and the first student steps forward. See you then.

sources.ref: Prashna Upanishad 1.1–1.2 (the six students; one more year; 'if we know')
